terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō), with ex and the ablative
evidence: Plaut. Am. 2.2.9: plūs aegrī ex abitū virī quam ex adventū voluptātis cēpī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With nouns of feeling and gain: voluptātem, dolōrem, frūctum capere ex. The verb’s first sense is “take, seize” (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō), with ex and the ablative
terms.comment: Literally to gather in (a harvest: percipere frūctūs, Cic. Sen. 24); also to perceive, learn. Somewhat weightier than capere.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with ex and the ablative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.3.1: molestiam trāxerit (Lewis & Short: “has derived, i.e. has received, suffered”)

phrases.latin: plūs aegrī ex abitū virī quam ex adventū voluptātis cēpī
phrases.english: I got more grief from my husband’s going than pleasure from his coming

phrases.latin: neque majōrem voluptātem ex īnfīnītō tempore aetātis percipī posse, quam ex hōc percipiātur
phrases.english: that no greater pleasure can be had from an endless lifetime than is had from this (finite) one
We get a lot of pleasure out of the garden.

tractum.html: Lachmann’s law does not lengthen before an old aspirate or a voiceless stop: the house ruling of 9 November 2026 (with Allen’s trăctus, against Bennett’s trāctus).

sources: Lewis & Short: capio · Lewis & Short: percipio · Lewis & Short: traho
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 361.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
